study.title: Ezekiel 22 The corrupt city, the slag and the absence of intercessor
study.overview: Ezekiel 22 presents three accusations linked to each other: the guilt of Jerusalem for shed blood and idolatry; the widespread corruption of leaders and people; and the final judgment of judgment because there was no one standing in the gap for the land. The chapter shows that sin was not only individual, but social and institutional: princes, priests, prophets and the whole people had perverted justice, worship and moral life. In response, the Lord announces dispersion, fire, melting in the furnace and consummation of his indignation. The culmination is the divine quest for an intercessor, unsuccessful, which makes judgment inevitable.

outline.title: Jerusalem is accused as a city of blood
outline.explanation: The prophet is sent as an accuser to expose the city's abominations. The text highlights shed blood, idolatry and public shame as signs of guilt before God and the nations.

outline.title: Leaders and people accumulate injustices and will receive dispersion
outline.explanation: Princes, family members, priests, merchants and citizens are described as violent, unclean and greedy. The consequence will be humiliation, dispersion among the nations, and recognition that the Lord is judging.

outline.title: The house of Israel is compared to slag in the oven
outline.explanation: Instead of useful gold or silver, Israel appears as mixed metal and worthless, destined for fire. The image does not promise restorative purification, but the destruction of what is useless and contaminated.

outline.title: Corruption of all groups and the lack of intercessor
outline.explanation: Prophets, priests, princes and people are denounced by conspiracy, lies, violence and theft. God seeks someone who puts himself in the breach, but finds no one; therefore his indignation will be poured out upon them.

study.context: The chapter is addressed to Jerusalem and the house of Israel as a community of covenant under trial. The given notes link various sins to God's law, especially prohibitions on violence, idolatry, sexual uncleanness, social injustice, and profanity of worship. The scenario is that of a people who have received spiritual privileges, but has transformed them into an occasion for wide corruption, including among religious and civil leaders.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God judges both sins against others and sins against his holiness. Blood spilled, idolatry, sexual abuse, economic exploitation and profane worship form a single network of rebellion. The representative responsibility of the leaders also appears: when they corrupt the people, judgment reaches the whole community. The image of the furnace shows that the divine judgment is holy and active; it is not merely emotional outburst, but a just response to persistent impurity. Finally, the search for someone who sets himself in the breach reveals the importance of intercession, and the absence of this mediator exposes the gravity of spiritual collapse. In evangelical reading, the text points to the need for a true intercessor, in contrast to the failure of human leaders, although the chapter itself emphasizes above all the sentence against Jerusalem.

scholarViews.insight: Judgment would not only be dispersion: God would also gather Judah in Jerusalem to be tested as metal in the furnace, but because it was slag, the result would be destruction and not purification.
The house of Israel, corrupt as slag, is presented as something useless that needs to be thrown into the fire; the image underlines the total degeneration of the community.
The final judgment comes because corruption has reached all classes to prophets, priests, princes, and people - so that divine indignation is fully justified.

questions: What forms of collective sin does this chapter help us to see today, in addition to individual faults?
In what ways can religious and civil leaders contribute to the guilt of a community rather than contain it?
What does it mean, in practice, to be in the breach by a family, church or city before God?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to the honest examination of public and personal life. Confess sins that involve injustice, uncleanness, and spiritual indifference; treat seriously the way you use power, influence, money, and words; and pray that God will raise people who intercede with courage and fidelity. It is also worth practicing concrete repentance: repairing damage when possible, abandoning dishonest gains and honoring the holiness of God in worship and daily life.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow us to safely state that the chapter denounces generalized sin and announces judgment; however, they do not authorize additional historical details beyond what the text itself and the comments say. The expression about "not receiving rain" in 22:24 appears in the notes as an image of divine indignation, but the exact meaning in the context is presented summarized by the commentators. It is also possible to read the image of the furnace in the key of refinement or destruction, but here I follow the majority emphasis of the notes, which underline consummation of the judgment on an irrecoverable slag.
